title: Describing a mood presentation: what changed, for how long, and who says so

objectives.statement: Write each element of a person's mood presentation so that it states what changed, over what period, and whether the person reported it, someone else reported it, or it was observed in the conversation.

Decide, for the depressive, elevated, irritable, mixed, psychotic, cognitive, sleep, energy, and functional elements, which are present, which are absent, and which were never established, and record the second and third of those as findings.
Describe a past episode reported from memory at the strength its source supports, giving its dates, its content, and its provenance, without converting it into a classification.

scenes.title: A line that nobody can check
scenes.contentHtml:
A line that nobody can check

A referral reaches the service the day before the appointment. Its clinical summary is one sentence:

34-year-old, four-month history of depression. Poor sleep, weight loss, reduced function. ?bipolar.

Nothing there is obviously wrong, and a colleague could read it in two seconds and picture the person. As evidence it is close to empty. Ask one question of each part: how would anybody check this?

  • Four-month history. Four months since what? Since the mood dropped, since the sleep changed, or since someone first said the word out loud?
  • Poor sleep. Poor in which direction? Trouble falling asleep, waking through the night, waking early and staying awake, or sleeping far more than usual?
  • Weight loss. Weighed, or estimated?
  • Reduced function. Reduced on whose account, measured against what this person was doing before?
  • ?bipolar. No part of that is a description. Somebody's conclusion has been written into the space where the evidence belongs.

In an hour you will meet R., who is 34 and works rotating night shifts in a warehouse. At the end of the conversation you have to produce something better than that sentence. Better does not mean longer. It means that a clinician who was not in the room can tell, for every single element, what changed, over what period, and where the information came from.

One word to settle before it causes trouble

Depression is two words sharing a spelling, and the two get swapped without anyone noticing.

In ordinary speech it names a low mood: I was depressed about the interview. Usually about something, usually passing, and no one means anything technical by it. In clinical use, a major depressive episode names a syndrome. Depressed mood or loss of interest and pleasure has to be present most days for at least two weeks, carrying several further changes alongside it: energy, sleep, concentration, guilt or a sense of worthlessness, movement, weight, thoughts of death. The syndrome also requires clinically significant distress, or impairment in social, occupational, or another important area. One area is enough; nothing requires that work, home life and self-care all give way together.

The referral used the second sense on evidence that would only support the first, and that happens constantly. This lesson writes low mood when it means the state and spells the syndrome out in full when it means the syndrome. Do the same in anything you write, and the ambiguity stops travelling.

What you are bringing with you

Check
id check-source-sorting

Earlier in this track you separated what a person tells you, what someone else tells you, what you see for yourself, and what you conclude. Retrieve it now, before you need it under time pressure. Sort these five fragments into those four kinds:

  1. "I wake at four and that's it."
  2. R. paused for about five seconds before most answers.
  3. The referring practice recorded 78 kg in March and 72 kg in July.
  4. R. is withdrawn.
  5. "My mates said I wouldn't shut up."

Write your four groups down before reading on.

One and five are R.'s own report, and they are not the same kind of report: the first is R. describing R.'s experience, the fifth is R. reporting what other people said six years ago. Two is your observation. Three is another person's record, and it is the only one of the five with a number that was taken by an instrument. Four is an inference. It is a reasonable one, and it belongs somewhere in your thinking, but it is not a finding and it cannot be checked by anyone who was not there.

That sorting is the whole method of this block. This lesson is where you use it on a full presentation and find out how much work it does.

Recovery route

Two earlier outcomes in this track carry the ideas above: separating a person's report, another person's report, direct observation, and inference; and describing a time-bound mental-status examination without collapsing it into shorthand. If your groups came out differently from the four above, you have not failed anything. Reread your own answers with this rule in hand: a finding is something a second clinician could have written down in the room, and a conclusion is something you added afterwards. That single rule recovers most of what those outcomes teach, and it is enough to work through this lesson.

Nothing here asks you to disclose anything about yourself. Every case is invented, and you can write your answers, dictate them, or talk them through with a tutor.

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary-open

Teaching example, not medical advice. R. is a fictional person built for this course, and so is every document quoted about R. Nothing in this lesson diagnoses anyone, recommends treatment, or describes what any real person should do. This course supports academic study and simulation; it confers no authority to assess or treat a real person.

Source Note
claims claim-depressive-episode-definitionsources source-carty-escalona-mdd

A review written for primary-care physicians supplies the clinical sense of the word: depressed mood or loss of interest as the necessary element, three or four further symptoms alongside it, present most days across at least two weeks, with dysfunction spread across work, home, self-care, and adherence. It describes United States practice under DSM-5 criteria. The everyday sense of the word is ordinary English and needs no source. The referral sentence, R., and the sorting exercise are inventions of this lesson.

scenes.title: Three things every element has to carry
scenes.contentHtml:
Three things every element has to carry

A description is built out of elements. An element is one change: the sleep, the appetite, the interest in things, the ability to hold a thought. Write each one so that it carries three things, and the description survives being read by somebody who was not there.

  1. What changed, said concretely enough that a second clinician could recognise it. "Wakes at about 04:00 and does not get back to sleep" beats "poor sleep" because it names a direction.
  2. Over what period, which means an onset, a duration, and a pattern. "Most nights since around March" gives a pattern and an onset, and the duration follows from them. "Recently" gives none of the three.
  3. From what source, which means one of exactly three things: R. said it, somebody else said it, or you saw it.

The third of those is the one that gets dropped, and it is the one that decides how much weight the element can bear.

The three sources, and the thing that is not a source

Source What it is How it fails
Self-report The person's account of their own experience Memory, mood-dependent recall, and what the person considers worth mentioning
Other-person report An informant, a referral letter, a clinical record, a measurement taken elsewhere The informant's vantage point, their stake in the account, and what they were never in a position to see
Observation What you saw or heard during a bounded stretch of time It samples minutes, and it tells you nothing about the other 23 hours

Inference belongs on none of those rows. "Withdrawn", "guarded", "poor insight", and "labile" are conclusions about a person drawn from findings, and a record that mixes them in with findings has stopped being checkable. Keep them, use them, and mark them as yours.

Two distinctions inside that table earn their keep almost immediately.

A person's report about another person is still their report. When R. says my mates told me I wouldn't shut up, you have R.'s memory of a remark, not the friends' account. It sits on the self-report row, and it is weaker than the rest of that row because it is second-hand inside a first-hand account.

A measurement taken elsewhere is stronger than either party's estimate. R. thinks the weight loss is "maybe six kilos". The referring practice weighed R. at 78 kg in March and 72 kg in July. Those are the same six kilograms, arrived at two different ways, and only one of them can be compared against a number taken in three months' time.

Time course is not decoration

An element without a time course cannot be compared with anything, including itself. Four things are worth pinning down, and none of them takes long to ask.

  • Onset. When did this start, and did it come on over days or over months? A person who can name the week is telling you something different from a person who cannot.
  • Duration. How long has it run without letting up?
  • Pattern. Is it worse at a particular time of day, on particular days, or continuously?
  • Direction. Getting worse, holding steady, or easing?

Then the part that people skip: put the dated elements next to each other. R.'s sleep changed around March. R.'s drinking increased over the last two months. The weight was 78 kg in March and 72 kg in July. R. works rotating night shifts and has done for years. Laying those on one line is description. Deciding which of them caused which is a different job, done in a later lesson, and it becomes possible only if this lesson's dates were recorded properly in the first place.

Absent, denied, and never asked

Three states, and only the middle one is usually written down.

If R. describes hearing voices, that is present. If you ask directly and R. says no, that is a finding: asked and denied. If nobody raised it, that is a gap in your assessment, and it is not the same as absence.

A record that goes silent on an element is telling the next reader nothing, and the next reader will usually assume it was absent. Write the negatives you actually established, and write the gaps as gaps.

Why the source tag is clinical and not clerical

Some things a person is well placed to report, and some things they are not. A patient's own account is the only route to what their mood feels like from inside. It is a much weaker route to a past period of raised activity, for reasons a later scene takes apart. A 2025 seminar on bipolar disorder puts the practical consequence plainly: establishing a hypomanic period from the patient's history alone is difficult, corroborative history helps confirm it, and the gap between a first diagnosis of unipolar depression and a diagnosis of bipolar disorder can run to about ten years.

That is what the source tag buys. It tells the next clinician which parts of the picture rest on the route most likely to have missed something, and where a second account would add the most.

Check
id check-three-tags

R. says: "I'm tired in a way that sleeping doesn't fix."

Write that as an element carrying all three things. You will have to notice what R. did not supply, and say so instead of inventing it.

A workable version: fatigue disproportionate to sleep, frequency and onset not established, R.'s report. The tiredness and its quality come from R., and nothing else does, because R. was asked neither how often nor since when. Writing "for four months" there would move a number from the sleep element onto the energy element, where nobody put it. Two short questions fix it, and until they are asked the honest line is the one with the holes visible.

Source Note
claims claim-corroborative-historysources source-singh-bipolar-seminar

A 2025 seminar in The Lancet supports the difficulty of establishing hypomania from the patient's account alone, the usefulness of corroborative history, and a delay of up to about ten years between a diagnosis of unipolar depression and one of bipolar disorder. Those figures describe cohorts of people who eventually received a bipolar diagnosis and say nothing about any individual. The three-source table, the four time-course questions, and R.'s numbers are this lesson's own construction.

scenes.title: Nine kinds of change, one person
scenes.contentHtml:
Nine kinds of change, one person

The outcome this lesson serves names nine kinds of change: depressive, elevated, irritable, mixed, psychotic, cognitive, sleep, energy, and functional. R. hands you some of them across the table, hands you one from memory, and leaves the rest for you to establish or rule out.

Learning the nine as a list is easy and close to useless. What matters is knowing, for each one, what you would be looking at, and what you write when it is not there. The full record of R.'s conversation arrives in the next scene; here it appears in fragments.

The ones R. gives you directly

Low mood is the element R. came about, so it arrives first and it arrives vaguely: "It started sometime in the spring. March, maybe April." Loss of interest and pleasure arrives second, and R. dates it later than the mood: "I used to fish every weekend. I haven't been since. I don't want to." Those two carry the weight, because the clinical syndrome needs at least one of them present most days across at least two weeks before anything else counts toward it.

The rest of the depressive picture travels with them and is asked about one element at a time: sleep, appetite and weight, energy, concentration, guilt or a sense of worthlessness, movement, and thoughts of death. R. describes changes in sleep, weight, and energy, and describes thoughts of death only when asked directly. R. says nothing about guilt. The change in movement is something you watch rather than something R. mentions, which already tells you that these elements do not all arrive by the same route.

Two of them are worth separating out because they behave differently from the rest.

Energy is not sleep. R. is tired in a way that sleeping does not fix, and R. is also waking at four. Those are two elements with two time courses, and folding them into "fatigue" hides the fact that one of them might move without the other.

Cognitive change is not just a complaint. R. asked twice in twenty minutes for a question to be repeated, and lost the thread of an answer once. Depressive episodes carry measurable change in attention, in memory and learning, in executive function, and in the speed of mental and physical processing, and clinical practice guidelines published in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry in 2025 record that residual deficits persist after a depressive episode resolves, with a documented effect on occupational and social functioning. Guidance reports that cognitive difficulty can persist for some people after the mood elements have resolved, which is not the same as saying it persists for everyone, and this lesson does not treat concentration as the element most likely to remain. So the concentration element needs its own line in the description and its own time course. It is one of the elements most likely to still be there at the next appointment when the mood has lifted.

Function is what the other elements did to the week. R. is still going to work. R. has had two write-ups for picking errors. R. has stopped answering friends. Function is a set of specific things that used to happen and now happen differently, each carrying its own date. A single global rating replaces all of that with one number that nobody can take apart again.

The one R. gives you from memory

Six years ago, by R.'s account, there were about five days of hardly sleeping, of doing a great deal, of unusual talkativeness, and of several purchases R. could not afford. Nobody assessed it. R. calls it a good patch.

What is being described there has a shape. A 2025 seminar on bipolar disorder sets it out as a distinct period of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood together with increased activity or energy, carrying some combination of reduced need for sleep, pressured or increased speech, racing ideas, distractibility, grandiosity, impulsivity, increased goal-directed activity, and involvement in things with a high potential for painful consequences. The conventional duration thresholds are at least seven days for mania, or less if it led to hospital admission, and at least four days for hypomania. Psychotic features occur in mania and are not part of hypomania.

Notice the two directions that period can take. Elevated and irritable are alternatives on the same element, and an episode of raised activity can present as either. R. describes the elevated version. Irritability on its own, with nothing else changed, tells you very little, because it accompanies a great many states; it counts for much more when it arrives with the raised activity, the shortened sleep, and a start date.

Whether R.'s five days clear any threshold, and what it would mean if they did, is the next lesson's question. What this lesson owes that episode is an accurate count of the days, a description of what actually happened during them, and an honest label saying that all of it comes from one person's memory of six years ago.

The two that change what kind of picture this is

Mixed features means depressive and elevated features running inside the same episode. A multicentre Korean chart review of 672 non-psychotic mood episodes found that how often this gets recorded depends heavily on which criteria are applied. On the same 672 episodes, 5.8% met the DSM-5 mixed-features specifier and 31.7% met broader research criteria, a fivefold gap produced by the definition and not by the patients. Among the broader cases, irritable mood was the commonest elevated feature, at 90.8%. That study also found that patients with depression and mixed characteristics were frequently classified as having anxious distress or a personality disorder instead. The bipolar seminar adds that anxiety, agitation, and irritability during mixed states both drive misdiagnosis and raise the risk of suicide, which is why a describer is expected to look for these features instead of waiting for them to announce themselves.

R. was asked about irritability and about any days in the four months when the mood lifted, and described none, and no agitation was observed. Those are findings, and they are worth a line each.

They do not settle the question. The DSM-5-TR specifier turns on at least three opposite-pole symptoms, and the list runs wider than elevation and irritability: it includes increased talkativeness, racing thoughts, increased goal-directed activity, decreased need for sleep, and inflated self-esteem, among others. Two of those were never asked about here, and the sleep change R. does describe is increased waking rather than a reduced need for sleep, which is a different thing. What the record supports is that two mixed features were asked about and described as absent. Writing no mixed features would go past the evidence, and the misclassification the same chart review found is what going past it tends to cost.

Psychotic features means delusions or hallucinations occurring within the mood episode. A review of psychotic depression records that the delusional content is commonly nihilistic, carrying the belief that something bad is about to happen, and that the rate is not small: in the United States Epidemiologic Catchment Area study, 14.7% of people meeting criteria for major depression had a history of psychotic features, a European sample put it at 18.5%, and about a quarter of hospitalised depressed patients met criteria for the psychotic form. Psychotic features are described as mood-congruent when their content fits the mood state and mood-incongruent when it does not, and current classification gives precedence to the incongruent features when both are present.

The reason to ask R. directly sits in the same review. Among 130 diagnoses in a well-characterised sample of people with psychotic depression, 27% were initially wrong, and what the assessing clinicians had missed was the psychosis and not the mood disorder. R. was asked and described nothing of the kind. That sentence goes in the record.

The nine, and what R.'s description can honestly say about each

Element Status for R. Source
Depressive (low mood) Present, most days, since about March R.'s report
Elevated Reported for about five days, six years ago R.'s memory, never assessed
Irritable Asked about the four months and denied R.'s report
Mixed No days of the mood lifting in the four months; no agitation seen R.'s report, and observation
Psychotic Asked and denied R.'s report
Cognitive Two requests to repeat a question and one lost thread, in twenty minutes Observed
Sleep Waking about 04:00, not returning to sleep, most nights other than late shifts R.'s report
Energy Fatigue not relieved by sleep; frequency and onset not established R.'s report
Functional Still at work; two picking errors written up; stopped seeing friends R.'s report

Seven of the nine rest on R.'s account alone. A description that says so is telling you exactly where it is thin, which is the reason the next lesson wants a second account.

Source Note
claims claim-depressive-episode-definition, claim-elevated-episode-features, claim-mixed-features, claim-psychotic-features-in-depression, claim-cognitive-changessources source-carty-escalona-mdd, source-singh-bipolar-seminar, source-shim-mixed-features, source-rothschild-psychotic-depression, source-singh-cognition-guideline

Five sources support the phenomenology above and each one limits what it can support. The primary-care review supplies the depressive elements and the two-week duration under DSM-5. The 2025 Lancet seminar supplies the elevated and irritable features and the mania and hypomania duration thresholds. The Korean multicentre chart review is a retrospective study of patients hospitalised across twelve centres, so its two prevalence figures describe that population and appear here to show how far the number moves with the criteria applied. The psychotic-depression review supplies the frequency figures, the nihilistic content, the congruence distinction, and the 27% initial-misdiagnosis finding from one well-characterised sample. The 2025 Indian Journal of Psychiatry guidelines supply the affected cognitive domains and the persistence of deficits after an episode resolves. R., the table, and every value in it are invented for this lesson.

scenes.title: Assembling R.'s description from the raw material
scenes.contentHtml:
Assembling R.'s description from the raw material

The conversation lasted twenty minutes. Here is everything it produced, in the order it arrived, plus the letter that came with the referral. Read it before the worked example, because the example works on exactly this and nothing else.

What R. said
S1 "It started sometime in the spring. March, maybe April. It's every day now."
S2 "I used to fish every weekend. I haven't been since. I don't want to."
S3 "I wake at four and that's it. I lie there till the alarm."
S4 "Most nights. Every night I'm not on a late."
S5 "I'm tired in a way that sleeping doesn't fix."
S6 "I've lost weight. Maybe six kilos. I'm not trying to."
S7 "I'm cold all the time. And I'm blocked up, if that matters."
S8 "Work's fine." Then, a few minutes later: "I've had two write-ups for picking errors. That's never happened to me."
S9 "I stopped answering my friends. It's easier."
S10 "I have a drink most evenings. More the last couple of months. It's the only thing that puts me under."
S11 "Six years back there were about five days where I hardly slept and I was flying. I redid the kitchen in a weekend. I bought a bike I couldn't afford. My mates said I wouldn't shut up. It was a good patch."
S12 "My mum had nerves. She was on lithium for years. I don't know what for."
S13 Asked directly: "Sometimes I think it wouldn't matter if I didn't wake up. I wouldn't do anything about it. I never have."
S14 Asked directly about unusual experiences and beliefs: R. described none.
S15 Asked directly about irritability, and about any days in the four months when the mood lifted: R. described none.

What was observed in the room
O1 Pauses of about five seconds before most answers.
O2 Speech quiet and slowed; answers short; no spontaneous conversation.
O3 Little change in facial expression across the twenty minutes, including while describing the bike.
O4 Sat still throughout, with little spontaneous movement.
O5 Asked for a question to be repeated twice, and lost the thread mid-answer once.
O6 Kept a coat on throughout, in a warm room.
O7 No tears.

What the referral letter says
L1 R. attended the practice in March and again in July.
L2 Weight 78 kg in March, 72 kg in July.
L3 The July entry records that R. reported waking early. The March entry records nothing about mood or sleep.
L4 No thyroid function test has been requested or performed.
L5 The letter says nothing about any period six years ago.
Worked Example
id worked-example-assemble-r

Task. Replace the referral's one-line summary with a description in which every element states what changed, over what period, and where it came from, and in which the negatives that were established are visible alongside the gaps that were not.

What you have and what you do not. Twenty-seven raw items across three sources. Missing: the onset of the fatigue, whether the loss of interest began with the low mood or after it, any account from a person who has watched R. across the four months, and a thyroid result.

Principle selected. Every element carries what changed, its time course, and its source, and inference is kept off the finding lines. It fits here because the raw material arrives in three provenances that fail in different ways, and a summary that merges them cannot be checked by anyone downstream.

Plan. Sort by source, group by element, write each element with its three tags, write the established negatives and the gaps, then test whether a clinician reading it in three months could tell what had moved.

Execution, and the decisions that shape it.

Sleep (S3, S4, L3). Direction, pattern, and a dated trace: waking at about 04:00 without returning to sleep, most nights other than nights worked late, since around March on R.'s account, with the practice's July entry recording R. making the same report to the general practitioner. That last clause is worth writing carefully. It establishes that R. was saying this in July, and it is not a second observer confirming it, because the practice recorded R.'s report and not anybody's observation. A record that says "corroborated by the GP" would have upgraded the same source twice. The shift pattern belongs in the line because a sleep description that ignores rotating nights describes the wrong week.

Energy (S5). Fatigue that sleep does not relieve, frequency and onset not established, R.'s report. The temptation is to write "most days, for four months" and borrow both numbers from the sleep element. Nobody asked, so nobody knows, and the honest line is shorter and more useful than the invented one.

Weight (S6, L2). Two versions of the same fact, and the description keeps both. R. estimates about six kilograms without trying. The practice recorded 78 kg in March and 72 kg in July. Only the second version can be compared against a number taken in October, so it is the one that carries the measurement and R.'s account is what tells you it was unintentional.

Function (S8, S9). R. says work is fine and also reports two written warnings for picking errors, the first in R.'s account of that job, plus stopping contact with friends. Both halves of S8 go in, unreconciled. Deciding that "work's fine" is minimisation is an inference, and writing it as a finding would delete the only quotation that shows how R. currently talks about work.

Mood and its expression (S1, S2, O3). R. describes daily low mood since about March, and loss of interest and pleasure in fishing dated later than the mood, though how much later was not established. Separately, and this is an observation and not a report, facial expression changed little across the twenty minutes, including while R. described the bike. Those are two different elements. Psychiatry keeps two words for them: mood is the sustained state the person reports from the inside, and affect is the moment-to-moment expression an observer watches, including its range and how it moves. The mental-status outcome earlier in this track owns that distinction, and this lesson uses it in exactly that sense. Keeping them on separate lines is what lets a later reader see when one moves without the other.

Cognition (O5). Asked for a question to be repeated twice and lost the thread once, across twenty minutes, observed. R. was not asked about concentration at home, so the element rests on an observation of a short sample and says so.

Psychomotor (O1, O2, O4). Long response latency, quiet slowed speech, little spontaneous movement, observed across twenty minutes. This is where the observation row earns its place: none of it came from R., and R. might not have reported any of it.

Physical (S7, L4). R. reports feeling cold constantly and being constipated. The letter records that no thyroid function test has been requested. The second sentence is a gap in the record, written as a gap. What to make of the pairing is not this lesson's question and guessing at it here would put an inference into a description.

Alcohol (S10). R.'s account: most evenings, increased over about two months, and R.'s stated reason is to get to sleep. Put the two dates side by side and stop. The sleep change is dated to around March and the increase in drinking to around May, so the drinking followed the sleep change in time. Writing which produced which is a causal claim, and a description that makes it has stopped describing.

The five days, six years ago (S11). About five days, hardly sleeping, high activity, a kitchen redecorated in a weekend, a bike bought that R. could not afford, and unusual talkativeness as reported to R. by friends at the time. Never assessed by anyone. R.'s framing, "a good patch", stays in the record as R.'s words, because how a person holds a past period is itself information. What does not go in the record is a diagnostic name for it.

Family (S12). R. reports that a parent had "nerves" and took lithium for years, and that R. does not know what it was for. Recorded exactly at that strength: R.'s second-hand account of a medicine, with the indication unknown to R.

Risk (S13). Passive thoughts that life would not be missed. R. said "I wouldn't do anything about it" and "I never have", which is R.'s reported current intention and R.'s reported history, and that is how the line records them. No question about a plan is documented anywhere in the material, so the description says the domain was not covered rather than writing a negative nobody obtained. R. raised none of this until asked directly, and that clause is part of the finding too. An unqualified no plan, no intent, no act would be the same failure this lesson spends its length naming: a tidy line that a later reader cannot check and that no one in the room actually established.

Asked and denied (S14, S15). R. described no hallucinations and no beliefs that others found strange, no irritability, and no days within the four months when the mood lifted. Three established negatives, written as findings, so the next reader knows which questions were put. The last of them also settles the mixed element, which cannot be described until somebody asks whether the mood ever went the other way.

Assumptions and limits. Everything from R. comes from one conversation on one day. The observations sample twenty minutes and are silent about the other twenty-three hours. The two weights were taken on practice scales at visits four months apart.

Independent check. Take each line and ask: who would have to be asked to confirm this? If a line has no answer, its source tag is missing. Run it and the description passes, with one instructive result: for seven of the nine elements the answer is "R.", which is a true statement about how thin the evidence is and a reason to seek a second account.

Interpretation. The description now supports three things it could not support before. There is a four-month picture with dated elements. There is a documented six-kilogram fall between two weighings. There is an unassessed five-day period six years ago, described at the strength of one person's memory. It supports none of the following: which element produced which, any classification of either period, and the referral's "?bipolar", which entered the record as somebody's conclusion and leaves it again because nothing in the raw material establishes it.

Self-explanation. Of the decisions above, which one most changes what a clinician in three months' time is able to do with this record?

A good answer picks the weight decision or the energy decision, and for the same reason. Keeping the practice's two weighings gives a later reader a number to compare against. Refusing to invent an onset for the fatigue leaves a hole that can still be filled by asking. Both decisions are about whether the record can be used again later, which is what separates a description from an impression.

Check
id check-what-changed

One line of the finished description reads:

Waking at about 04:00 without returning to sleep, most nights other than nights worked late, since around March by R.'s account, and recorded again in the practice notes in July, where it is the same self-report on a second date rather than a second source.

Rewrite it as the referral would have: "poor sleep". Then name three specific questions that a clinician in October can answer from the first version and cannot answer from the second.

The first version answers: has the waking time moved, has the frequency moved, and is R. now getting back to sleep. The second version answers none of them, because it never recorded a direction, a rate, or a baseline. That is the entire practical difference between the two records, and it arrives three months after anyone stopped thinking about the wording.

Source Note
claims claim-depressive-episode-definition, claim-retrospective-report-is-evidencesources source-carty-escalona-mdd, source-birk-retrospective-validity

The primary-care review supports the depressive elements the assembly asks about, including the direction of the sleep and weight changes and the two-week duration under DSM-5. The study of retrospectively reported depressive episodes supports treating R.'s account of six years ago as evidence with soft edges: among 68 participants in a long-running Oregon cohort, symptom scores collected at the time were higher during periods later reported as episodes than between them by a medium-to-large margin, and 49.1% of those contemporaneous within-episode reports reached the scale's clinical cut-off. That study examined depressive episodes in one United States cohort, so it supports the general point that a remembered episode carries real signal and imprecise boundaries; it does not measure how accurately anyone recalls a period of raised activity. R., the transcript, the observations, and the letter are inventions of this lesson.

scenes.title: When the tags fall off
scenes.contentHtml:
When the tags fall off

Here is R.'s presentation written the way most records are written. It is fluent, it is quick to read, and a competent clinician produced it.

34-year-old warehouse worker with a four-month history of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep, low energy, weight loss and reduced function. History of a hypomanic episode six years ago. Drinking to sleep. Family history of bipolar disorder. Passive suicidal ideation. No psychosis.

Check
id check-what-the-paragraph-lost

Before reading on, commit to an answer. Name two things in that paragraph that are now stated more strongly than the evidence behind them, and one thing that a clinician in three months' time can no longer check.

The model that produces it

The paragraph comes from a defensible idea: a description is a piece of clinical writing whose job is to convey the picture, and provenance is bookkeeping that a careful reader can reconstruct or that can be filled in later if it turns out to matter.

That idea is held widely, and it is not stupid. Clinical time is short, and the paragraph does convey a picture. What it cannot do is survive contact with a second reader.

Two of its lines have changed status on the way in.

"History of a hypomanic episode six years ago." Nobody assessed that period. The raw material was one person's memory of five days, offered as a good patch. The paragraph has turned a retrospective self-report into a clinical history, and the next clinician has no way to tell, because the sentence that would have told them was the sentence that got trimmed.

"Family history of bipolar disorder." R. reported that a parent had "nerves" and took lithium for years, with the indication unknown to R. The paragraph has converted a second-hand memory of a medicine into a diagnosis in a relative.

Two more have lost a qualifier. "Poor sleep" no longer says that R. wakes at about 04:00 and stays awake, so a clinician in October cannot tell whether R.'s sleep improved, worsened, or changed shape. And "passive suicidal ideation" no longer says that R. raised none of it until asked directly, which is the part of that finding a duty clinician at two in the morning would most want to know.

Why the first of those is the expensive one

There is a real finding underneath R.'s "a good patch", and the paragraph destroys the ability to use it.

A Dutch general-population study re-interviewed 40 adults with a confirmed lifetime bipolar diagnosis and asked what they thought had happened to them. 82.5% recognised having had a depressive episode. 22.5% recognised having had a hypomanic or manic one, and 17.5% had ever consulted a health professional about it. The people who did not recognise those periods explained them as pleasant and productive stretches, as part of their personality, or as the result of circumstances.

Read R.'s wording against that list. "It was a good patch" is close to the first explanation, and that is a reason to take the account seriously and to write it down in full.

The same finding is why the account cannot be promoted. In that study the episodes were established by a structured diagnostic interview, and roughly three in four participants did not recognise the raised-activity periods at all. R. has had no such interview. What exists is the account, and an account is a real piece of evidence. How good a piece is a separate question, and the work available here does not settle it. Studies of retrospectively reported depressive episodes show that periods people later name as episodes were genuinely worse at the time by contemporaneous measurement, though only about half of those contemporaneous reports reached the measure's clinical threshold. That is reassuring about one kind of recall and it is not evidence about this one. The reappraisal work in this same scene points the other way for raised activity, which is recognised far less reliably than low mood. So the account is kept, and its edges are kept visible with it. A record that says "reports about five days" preserves both facts. A record that says "history of hypomania" preserves neither.

The repair

Misconception
id misconception-strength-drift

The incorrect model. A description is a fluent summary of the clinical picture; where each part came from is bookkeeping that can be reconstructed by the reader or added later.

Where it fails. Provenance cannot be reconstructed downstream. Once "reports about five days six years ago, never assessed" becomes "history of hypomania", every subsequent reader inherits the stronger claim, and nothing in the record signals the loss. The same trimming turns a remembered medicine into a diagnosed relative, and a described sleep pattern into an undirected complaint.

The better model. The strength of a written statement is set by its source and its time course, and you write it at that strength. Where the source is thin, the sentence gets longer, and that is the sentence doing its job.

The same five days, three ways.

Version What it asserts What a later clinician can do with it
"History of hypomania." That an episode occurred and was identified as such Act on a diagnosis nobody made, and never learn that it was not made
"No history of mania." That the question was asked and settled in the negative Stop asking, on the strength of an established negative that was never established
"Reports about five days six years ago of markedly reduced sleep with increased activity, several purchases R. could not afford, and talkativeness noticed by friends at the time. Never assessed. R. describes it as 'a good patch'." That R. gave this account, with this content, about this period Seek an informant who was there, ask what the friends noticed, and compare any future period against a described baseline

Recheck. R. also said: "My mum had nerves. She was on lithium for years. I don't know what for." Write the version of that line which asserts exactly what is known. Then say what a later clinician can do with your version that they could not do with "family history of bipolar disorder".

A workable answer: R. reports that a parent had what R. calls "nerves" and took lithium for a number of years; R. does not know the indication. A later clinician can now ask R.'s family, or request the parent's records with consent, because your line makes visible that there is something still to find out. The shorter version hides the question by appearing to have answered it.

Source Note
claims claim-hypomania-self-recognition, claim-retrospective-report-is-evidencesources source-regeer-self-recognition, source-birk-retrospective-validity

The Dutch reappraisal study supports the recognition figures, the consultation figure, and the explanations participants gave for periods they did not recognise. Its sample is 40 adults drawn from one general-population survey, so the percentages describe that sample rather than any clinic population, and the design compares self-recognition against a structured research interview. The Oregon cohort study supports the point that periods later reported as depressive episodes were measurably worse at the time, and that fewer than half of the contemporaneous reports inside those periods reached the measure's clinical cut-off; it studied depressive episodes and does not measure recall of raised activity. R.'s wording and the three versions of the five days are this lesson's own.

scenes.title: Tag it, finish it, write it
scenes.contentHtml:
Tag it, finish it, write it

Three tasks, with less help each time. Write your answers before reading the response under each one. M. and K. are invented, like everyone else in this lesson.

1. Tag the source

M. is 52 and drives a delivery van. These six items came out of one appointment.

  1. "I've been flat since my father died in the spring."
  2. M.'s daughter, who came in, says M. has not cooked a meal since June.
  3. M. answered every question within a second and at normal volume.
  4. "I sleep fine. Nine, ten hours. I could sleep all day."
  5. The occupational health report records two absence episodes totalling eleven days since April.
  6. M. seemed to be minimising.

For each item, give its source, and mark the ones that arrive without a time course.

Response. Items 1 and 4 are M.'s report. Item 2 is another person's report, and note what kind: the daughter is reporting an observation of her own, over months, which is a vantage point M. does not have on M.'s own cooking. Item 3 is your observation, and it is the one people forget to write down because nothing was wrong with it; a normal response latency in a person describing low mood is a finding worth recording, and it distinguishes M. from R. Item 5 is another person's record and the only item carrying a counted quantity. Item 6 is an inference, and it belongs in your impression rather than on a finding line.

Time courses: items 1, 2 and 5 state one, and item 3 carries the appointment itself as its window, which is all an observation ever has. Item 4 arrives with none, and it needs the most work, because "I sleep fine" plus ten hours plus wanting to sleep all day is a change in the opposite direction from R.'s, and nobody has yet established when it started. The question does not apply to item 6, which is a conclusion and not an element.

If you tagged item 2 simply as "collateral", go back and say what the daughter was in a position to see. An informant's value is set by their vantage point, and "has not cooked since June" is a strong item precisely because she was there for it.

2. Repair four defective lines

Each of these lines has one defect, and it is a different defect each time. Name the defect and rewrite the line, inventing nothing.

Line as written
a Sleep disturbance for several months.
b Has not been managing at work.
c Poor insight into the severity of the illness.
d (the record says nothing at all about unusual experiences)

Response.

  • (a) No direction. Sleeping more and sleeping less are opposite findings that this line cannot tell apart. Rewrite once the direction is known: sleeping nine to ten hours and wanting more, since a date to be established, M.'s report.
  • (b) No source, and no specifics. Whose account is this? Rewrite: two absence episodes totalling eleven days since April, occupational health record. M. has not been asked about work directly.
  • (c) An inference sitting on a finding line. Move it to your impression, and put the finding it rests on where the finding belongs.
  • (d) Silence. A reader will take it as absence. If the question was asked, write the established negative. If it was not, write that it was not asked, and then ask it.

3. Write three elements from scratch

K. is 27 and was brought in by a housemate. This is all you have.

  • The housemate says K. has been "on one" for about three weeks: awake most of the night, out of the flat before six, talking over everyone.
  • K. says: "I've been getting a lot done. I've had maybe four hours a night and I don't need more."
  • K. says the last two weeks have also included "crying in the mornings, for no reason".
  • Observed across the appointment: speech fast and difficult to interrupt; four changes of topic in about two minutes; K. stood up twice.
  • Nobody has asked K. about unusual experiences or beliefs.

Write the sleep element, the elevated element, and the functional element, each with what changed, its period, and its source. Then write the one line that records a gap.

Response. A workable set:

  • Sleep: about four hours a night for roughly three weeks, described by K. as sufficient. K.'s report, with the housemate independently reporting that K. is awake most of the night and out of the flat before six over the same period.
  • Elevated: raised activity and rate of speech for about three weeks by both accounts, with reduced need for sleep and increased talkativeness. K.'s report and the housemate's report; pressured, hard-to-interrupt speech and frequent topic change observed in the appointment. K. also reports crying in the mornings over the last two weeks, so depressive and elevated features are described as running together in the last fortnight.
  • Functional: out of the flat before six and talking over others, three weeks, housemate's report. No information about work or study.
  • Gap: unusual experiences and beliefs not asked about.

Two things separate a strong answer from a passable one. The first is that the reduced need for sleep is written as an element in its own right, because K. describing four hours as enough is different from K. lying awake wishing for more, and that difference is what "reduced need" names. The second is the last fortnight: crying in the mornings inside a three-week period of raised activity is a described co-occurrence, and it goes in the record as a co-occurrence with both dates. Naming what kind of episode that makes is not this lesson's task and not yet possible from this material.

If your answer named an episode type for K., go back to the previous scene and rewrite the five-days table for K.'s three weeks. If your elements came out without periods attached, redo task 1 first; the tagging habit has to be automatic before the writing gets fluent.

Callout
id callout-practice-recovery

Every task above can be retried on new material without replaying the same answers. For task 1, take any six items from R.'s raw material in the earlier scene and tag those instead. For task 3, write the three elements for M. rather than K., which forces the opposite direction of sleep change and an informant with a different vantage point.

Source Note
claims claim-depressive-episode-definition, claim-elevated-episode-featuressources source-carty-escalona-mdd, source-singh-bipolar-seminar

The primary-care review supports the depressive elements the tasks ask about, including sleep in either direction and the two-week minimum duration under DSM-5. The Lancet seminar supports the elevated features K.'s material contains: raised activity or energy, reduced need for sleep, and increased talkativeness within a distinct period. Neither source is being used to classify K., M., or R. M. and K. are inventions of this lesson.

scenes.title: Reading a description you did not write
scenes.contentHtml:
Reading a description you did not write

Everything so far assumed you were in the room. Most of the time you are not. A document arrives about somebody you have never met, and you have to work out what it actually establishes before you can add anything to it.

P. is 61 and spent eight days on a general medical ward after a fall. This is the mental-health content of the discharge summary, quoted in full.

Low mood noted by nursing staff. Patient reports poor appetite. Slept poorly on the ward. Agitated overnight on day 2, settled with reassurance. Historically had a breakdown in P.'s 30s. Weight on admission 61 kg. Declined food on three occasions (nursing notes). Cognitive screen not performed. Seen by liaison psychiatry day 5: no acute mental health needs.

Your task

Working only from that paragraph:

  1. Write the elements it genuinely supports, each with its source and whatever time course it carries.
  2. Name every place where the document withholds the source.
  3. Say which of the nine elements you cannot populate at all, and separate "the document says it was absent" from "the document is silent".
  4. List, in order, the three things you would ask for first.

Write your answers before reading on.

What the paragraph supports

Three lines carry a source and can be used as they stand. Declined food on three occasions is an other-person report of a countable observation, and it is the strongest item in the document because somebody counted. Agitated overnight on day 2 is an other-person report of an observation with a date attached, and the document does not say whether it recurred on any other night. Weight on admission 61 kg is a measurement, so it is usable as a baseline for the next weighing while establishing nothing at all about change so far, because no earlier weight exists to set it against. A number with nothing behind it is a starting point and not a time course.

Two lines look like findings and are not. Low mood noted by nursing staff has a source and no date, no duration, and no description of what was noted; "noted" could cover a single remark or eight days of observation. Seen by liaison psychiatry day 5: no acute mental health needs is a conclusion, correctly dated and correctly attributed, which is a different kind of thing from a finding and cannot substitute for one. It tells you what another team decided on day 5 about the question they were asked. It does not tell you what they saw.

One line has had its source removed. Historically had a breakdown in P.'s 30s could be P.'s own account, a relative's, or a sentence copied from an old letter, and the three would carry very different weight. "Breakdown" is a lay word covering a wide range of events, and by itself it names nothing. This is the same defect that turned R.'s five days into a history of hypomania, arriving from the other direction: there, a weak source was written strongly; here, the source has simply been deleted.

What the document cannot tell you

Element State
Depressive (low mood) Reported by staff, undated, undescribed
Elevated, irritable, mixed Silent
Psychotic Silent
Cognitive Explicitly not assessed, and the document says so
Sleep Poor on the ward; direction and pre-admission pattern silent
Energy Silent
Functional Silent apart from the fall

Not one row in the document records an established negative. The cognitive row comes closest, because somebody wrote down that the screen was not performed, and recording a gap that way is better practice than most of the paragraph. Every other silence is unreadable. Nobody can tell whether P. was asked about unusual experiences and said no, or was never asked. That distinction is not academic: in one well-characterised sample of people with psychotic depression, 27% of diagnoses were initially wrong, and what the assessing clinicians had missed was the psychosis rather than the mood disorder. A silence in a record is precisely how that happens twice.

The three things to ask for, in order: who said "breakdown", and what happened; what the nursing notes actually describe under "low mood", with dates; and whether anyone has weighed P. before. The first is first because it is the only line that could change the shape of the picture, and because it is the cheapest to establish. Establishing a past period from the patient's account alone is unreliable, so the question runs past what P. says now to who else was there at the time.

Accessibility and alternatives

Every task in this lesson is text in and text out, and nothing depends on seeing a layout, a colour, or a diagram. The tables restate information that the surrounding prose also states, so a reader using a screen reader loses nothing by reading the prose alone. Answers can be written, dictated, recorded, or worked through aloud with a tutor; the assessment rubric scores the reasoning and does not reward a particular format. If reading a long quoted document is difficult, work through the discharge paragraph one sentence at a time against the three questions in the first section, since each sentence is independently assessable.

Nothing in this lesson requires you to disclose your own health, mood, sleep, or history, and no task asks you to describe a real person.

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary-transfer

Teaching example, not medical advice. P. is invented, and so is the discharge summary. The exercise is about what a document establishes, and it is not a judgement of any real clinician's record-keeping or a template for real clinical practice.

Source Note
claims claim-psychotic-features-in-depression, claim-corroborative-historysources source-rothschild-psychotic-depression, source-singh-bipolar-seminar

The psychotic-depression review supports the 27% initial-misdiagnosis figure and the finding that what was missed was the psychosis rather than the mood disorder; it describes one well-characterised research sample and is used here to show what an unreadable silence costs, not to estimate how often records are wrong. The Lancet seminar supports the difficulty of establishing a past raised-activity period from the patient's account alone and the value of corroborative history. P. and the discharge summary are inventions of this lesson.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: eleven weeks later, has anything changed?
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: eleven weeks later, has anything changed?

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary-wrapup

Teaching example, not medical advice. R. is fictional, and every number below was invented to make a point about records. Nothing here describes a real person's course, and nothing here is a basis for anyone's care.

This is the question the description was built to answer, and it is a medical question before it is a clerical one. R. is seen again eleven weeks after the first appointment, by a clinician who was not there the first time. Suppose that appointment produces the following.

  • The practice weighed R. in October: 73.5 kg, on the same scales as the July reading of 72 kg.
  • R. says: "I still wake at four, but maybe three nights a week now. Twice I got back off."
  • R. says: "I still haven't called anyone."
  • R. says there have been no further write-ups.
  • R. says the drinking is down to two evenings a week.
  • Observed: answers came within a second or two; facial expression still changed little across the appointment; no coat this time.
  • Not asked at this appointment: when the fatigue began, whether the interest in fishing has moved, or anything about concentration.
  • Still no thyroid function result.

Now put the two possible baselines side by side and answer the question from each.

From the referral's version

34-year-old, four-month history of depression. Poor sleep, weight loss, reduced function. ?bipolar.

Nothing can be said. Not "improved", not "unchanged", not "worse". "Poor sleep" has no direction, so three nights of early waking cannot be compared with whatever it stood for. "Weight loss" has no number, so 73.5 kg compares with nothing. "Reduced function" has no source and no specifics, so "no further write-ups" attaches to nothing. And "?bipolar" is still sitting in the record eleven weeks later, having never been evidence and never having been withdrawn.

The eleven weeks have produced real information and there is no instrument in the record to read it with.

From the description you built

Five statements about change become available, and each one carries its own strength.

  1. Weight is up 1.5 kg between July and October, both readings taken on the same practice scales. Two measurements from one instrument, so the comparison is as good as the instrument.
  2. Early waking has fallen from most nights to about three a week, and returns to sleep are now occurring where previously they were not. Both the baseline and the follow-up are R.'s report, so this compares like with like. That is the condition that makes the comparison legitimate. Setting an observation against a self-report, or a nurse's account against a patient's, produces a difference that may belong to the source and not to the person.
  3. Response latency has fallen from about five seconds to one or two. Observed both times, and observed by two different clinicians, so the comparison is weaker than the weight and should say so in the record.
  4. Facial expression changed little on both occasions. One observed element has moved and another has not, and that is visible only because they were written on separate lines.
  5. Social contact is unchanged, and work has had no further written warnings, both on R.'s account, with no employer's account at either time point.

Three elements cannot be compared at all. Energy has no baseline frequency or onset and was not re-asked. Interest and pleasure was not re-asked. Concentration was observed once and never tested. Two of those gaps were created at the first appointment, and one was created at the second. Both kinds are worth naming, because the fix is different: one is a writing problem and the other is an asking problem.

Why this is the medical point and not the administrative one

The description is the instrument. Change in a mood presentation is not measured by an assay; it is measured by comparing two descriptions, and a description without directions, dates, and sources has no scale on it.

The concentration gap shows what that costs. Clinical practice guidelines published in 2025 record that cognitive deficits in depression persist after the episode resolves, with a documented effect on occupational and social functioning. Suppose R.'s mood lifts over the next three months and R. still cannot hold a picking list. A record that folded concentration into "depression" will show improvement while R.'s job is still at risk, and nobody will be able to see the discrepancy, because the two things were never separately described. Separating them at baseline is what makes the lag visible later.

The same logic governs the five days six years ago. Described properly, they are a dated account of a specific period from a named source, carrying the strength that a remembered episode carries: real signal, with edges soft enough that the count of days may be wrong. That is still something a future period of raised activity can be compared against. Written as "history of hypomania", the five days become an assertion that no future evidence can either confirm or dislodge.

What this hands on

You can now describe a mood presentation across nine kinds of change, with a time course and a source on every element, and you can say what a record establishes and what it only appears to establish.

What none of that settles is what the picture is. The four-month low mood is the obvious reading, and three things sit against it: the five days six years ago that nobody assessed, the physical symptoms with no thyroid result behind them, and an alcohol pattern that is dated later than the sleep change. Weighing those against each other is the next outcome in this module, which distinguishes unipolar, bipolar-spectrum, medical, medication, substance, grief, trauma, and contextual alternatives using longitudinal evidence. It can only do that work on a description that kept its dates and its sources, which is why this lesson comes first.

Two places where this returns. When you next describe risk in a mood presentation, every element of it will need the same three tags, and "raised only on direct questioning" will be the tag that matters most. When you reach communicating and updating a formulation, the thing being updated is exactly the record you have just learned to write; a formulation built on untagged findings cannot be revised, because nobody can tell which part of it moved.

Recovery route

If the follow-up comparison above was hard to produce, the problem is almost never the follow-up. Go back to the worked assembly and check whether each of your elements carried a direction and a source. An element that reads "poor sleep" or "low energy" will always fail this scene, and it will fail it in a real clinic in the same way. Rebuild two elements with all three tags, then return here and answer the question again for those two alone.

Source Note
claims claim-depressive-episode-definition, claim-cognitive-changes, claim-retrospective-report-is-evidencesources source-carty-escalona-mdd, source-singh-cognition-guideline, source-birk-retrospective-validity

The primary-care review supports the depressive elements being compared across the two appointments, including sleep, weight, energy, and function. The 2025 Indian Journal of Psychiatry guidelines support the persistence of cognitive deficits after a depressive episode resolves and their effect on occupational and social functioning; the guidance addresses major depressive disorder and is used here to explain why concentration needs its own line, not to predict R.'s course. The Oregon cohort study supports treating a remembered episode as evidence with real signal and imprecise boundaries. Every number in the follow-up is invented for this lesson.

assessment.title: Describing a mood presentation: mastery check

items.prompt: D. is 45 and works as a school caretaker. This is everything the appointment produced. D. says: "I've not been right since the new year. Can't be bothered with anything." D. says: "I'm in bed by nine and I still can't get up. Ten, eleven hours." A note from D.'s line manager, dated last month, records four late arrivals in six weeks. Observed across the appointment: D. spoke at normal rate and volume, and cried while describing the job. D. was not asked about weight, about appetite, or about any past period of raised activity. Write four elements covering mood and interest, sleep, function, and observed expression. Each element must state what changed, its time course, and its source. Then write the line or lines that record what is missing.

answer.correct: Mood and interest: D.'s words are "I've not been right since the new year" and "Can't be bothered with anything", recorded as D.'s report, with an onset of around the new year and no course established. Lowered mood is not stated in those words and loss of interest is a reading of the second phrase rather than a quotation of it, so both are marked as needing a direct question rather than written in as findings. "Since the new year" gives an onset; it does not establish that anything has been continuous. Sleep: sleeping about ten to eleven hours with difficulty rising, in bed by about 21:00, onset not established, D.'s report; the direction is increased sleep. Function: four late arrivals in six weeks up to last month, line manager's record, which is another person's record and the only counted item here. Observed expression: tearful while describing the job; speech at normal rate and volume across the appointment; observed. Gaps: weight and appetite were not asked about, and no question was put about any past period of raised activity, so neither is an established negative.
answer.summary: Four elements, each with a change, a period, and a source, plus two recorded gaps.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for all four elements carrying a source that is one of self-report, another person's report, or observation, with the line manager's note correctly identified as another person's record. Award one point for the time courses, including writing that the sleep onset was not established instead of borrowing the new year from the mood element. Award one point for the two gaps written as gaps, and for the sleep element carrying its direction, which is increased sleep and the opposite of the case worked in the lesson. A response that writes 'sleep disturbance' without a direction does not earn the third point, because that line cannot be compared with anything at a later appointment. On a retry, use a different set: a person whose partner reports three months of early waking, who reports sleeping normally, whose employer's record shows no absence, and who was asked about unusual experiences and described none. The commonest failure on this item is to convert two ordinary phrases into syndrome language and a course. Credit is for recording what D. said, attributing it, and naming what is still unasked.
acceptableResponses: Any response giving four elements each with a change, a period, and one of the three sources, marking the sleep onset as not established, giving the sleep change a direction, and recording the unasked questions as gaps rather than as absences.
commonErrors: Borrowing the new year onset from the mood element onto the sleep element
Writing 'sleep disturbance' or 'poor sleep' without saying that D. is sleeping more
Recording the unasked questions as negatives, or leaving them out entirely
Treating the line manager's note as D.'s report, or as an observation of the assessor

items.prompt: A. is 38, and A.'s partner made the appointment. The partner says A. has been "flat and snappy" since about January and has stopped going to five-a-side football. A. says the sleep is "the same as always, six hours" and that work is unaffected. A. was tearful twice during the appointment and answered at normal speed. A. was asked about unusual experiences and beliefs and described none. Nobody asked about past periods of raised activity, about appetite, or about thoughts of death. For each of the nine kinds of change this lesson covers, say whether it is present, established as absent, or unaddressed by the record, and give the source wherever there is one. Then name the two questions you would ask first and say why those two.

answer.correct: Depressive: present since about January on the partner's report; A. has not described low mood directly, and the record keeps both accounts. Irritable: present since about January on the partner's report, unconfirmed by A. Elevated: unaddressed, never asked. Mixed: cannot be stated, because it depends on the elevated question that has not been put. Psychotic: established as absent, asked and denied. Cognitive: unaddressed. Sleep: A. reports about six hours and no change; the partner has not been asked, so this rests on one account. Energy: unaddressed; stopping five-a-side is suggestive and is a functional item, not an energy finding. Functional: stopped five-a-side since about January on the partner's report, and work unaffected on A.'s report. Observed: tearful twice, normal response speed, across one appointment. Ask first about any past period of raised activity, because it is the only unasked question that could change the shape of the whole picture and because the mixed question depends on it; and about thoughts of death, because it is unaddressed and because people was not raised until it was asked about directly, which is itself part of the finding.
answer.summary: Three present on the partner's report, one established negative, four unaddressed, one self-reported as unchanged, and two priority questions with reasons.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for separating the unaddressed elements from the single established negative, which requires noticing that only the psychotic element was asked and answered. Award one point for correct sourcing throughout, including keeping the partner's account of low mood and A.'s silence on it side by side without resolving them, and for not converting the football into an energy finding. Award one point for the two priority questions with reasons that turn on what the answer could change, rather than on completeness. A response that lists all four unaddressed elements as absent does not earn the first point. On a retry, use a case where the person reports the low mood and the informant disagrees, and where cognitive change is the only element that was asked about.
acceptableResponses: Any response that separates unaddressed from established-absent, sources every populated element, refuses to state the mixed element until the elevated question is asked, and justifies two priority questions by what their answers could change.
commonErrors: Recording the four unasked elements as absent
Resolving the disagreement between A. and the partner instead of recording both
Reading 'stopped five-a-side' as an energy finding rather than a functional one
Choosing the two priority questions for completeness rather than for what an answer would change

items.prompt: A person tells you: "About four years ago I had a fortnight where I barely slept, started three jobs round the house and finished none of them, and my sister said I was talking nonsense at her down the phone at two in the morning. I felt great. I never saw anyone about it." Write the line that belongs in the record. Then write what a clinician reading your line in a year's time can do that they could not do if the line read "history of a hypomanic episode four years ago".

answer.correct: Reports a period of about two weeks roughly four years ago with markedly reduced sleep, several household projects started and not completed, and speech that a sister described at the time as talking nonsense during a call at two in the morning. Describes feeling great during it. Never assessed by any clinician. Source: the person's retrospective account, with the sister's remark reported second-hand within it. A clinician reading that in a year can seek the sister as an informant, ask what she noticed and over how many days, and compare any new period of raised activity against a described baseline. The shorter version supports none of that, because it asserts an assessment nobody made and hides both the source and the content, so the next reader has nothing to check and no reason to check it.
answer.summary: A dated, sourced, contentful line, plus the three things it makes possible that a diagnostic label removes.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for the line carrying duration, dating, and specific content instead of a category. Award one point for the source being written as a retrospective self-report that was never assessed, with the sister's comment identified as second-hand inside that account rather than as an informant's report. Award one point for naming at least two concrete things a later reader can do, at least one of which is seeking the informant or establishing the duration more exactly. A response that writes the line well and then justifies it only by saying that it is more accurate does not earn the third point, because the value of the longer line is what it makes possible later. On a retry, do the same for a person who reports 'three or four days of not needing sleep' during a bereavement two years ago, where the dating is vaguer and one further source exists.
acceptableResponses: Any response whose recorded line gives duration, approximate date, described content, and the retrospective self-report source, and which names at least two later actions the line supports.
commonErrors: Writing a classification such as hypomania, mania, or a bipolar-spectrum label into the record line
Treating the sister's remark as an informant's report rather than as second-hand content inside the person's own account
Dropping the person's own framing of the period, which is itself information
Recording that the period was never assessed but then writing the rest of the line as established fact

items.prompt: A person is seen again three months after a first appointment. Which line from the first appointment supports a statement about whether that element has changed?

options.text: Waking at about 05:00 and not returning to sleep, five or six nights a week, since March, on the person's own account.
Limited insight into the extent of the difficulties.

answer.summary: Only the sleep line carries a direction, a rate, a start date, and a source, so it can be set against the same measurement three months later.
answer.reasoning: The sleep line names what changed, how often, since when, and who says so, which is what makes a later comparison possible on like terms. 'Appetite reduced' has no rate, no date, and no source. 'Marked fatigue, longstanding' has an intensity word doing the work of a time course, and longstanding gives no start point. 'Limited insight' is an inference and not a finding at all, so a change in it would be a change in the assessor's judgement. Feedback for a wrong choice: reread the four time-course questions, and check each option for a direction and a start date before checking anything else.
commonErrors: Choosing the fatigue line because 'longstanding' looks like a time course
Choosing the insight line because it sounds like a clinical judgement worth tracking
Choosing the appetite line because reduced names a direction, without noticing the missing rate, date, and source

rubrics.title: Elements with change, period, and source

criteria.description: All four elements carry one of the three sources, and the line manager's note is identified as another person's record.
Time courses are given where established and marked as not established where they are not, without borrowing a date from another element.
The sleep change carries its direction, and the unasked questions are recorded as gaps rather than as negatives or silence.

rubrics.title: Present, established absent, or unaddressed across the nine

criteria.description: Unaddressed elements are separated from the single established negative, and silence is never reported as absence.
Every populated element carries its source, the two accounts of the low mood are kept side by side, and the functional item is not converted into an energy finding.
Two priority questions are chosen and justified by what their answers could change, including the dependency of the mixed element on the elevated question.

rubrics.title: A remembered period held at the strength of its source

criteria.description: The recorded line carries duration, approximate dating, and specific described content instead of a category.
The source is written as a retrospective self-report never assessed, with second-hand content inside it identified as such.
At least two concrete later actions are named that the line supports and a diagnostic label would prevent.

rubrics.title: Recognising a line that can be compared

criteria.description: Selects the line carrying direction, rate, start date, and source.
