claims.statement: In clinical use a major depressive episode names a syndrome: depressed mood or loss of interest and pleasure present most days for at least two weeks, carrying several further changes alongside it across energy, sleep, concentration, guilt or worthlessness, psychomotor activity, weight, and thoughts of death, with dysfunction spread across work, home life, and self-care.
claims.scope: The DSM-5 construct as summarised for primary-care physicians in the United States in 2016. The lesson uses it to name which changes a description has to ask about, and never to classify a case.
claims.uncertainty: Classification systems differ in detail: ICD-11 and DSM-5 do not align element for element, and the criteria have been revised repeatedly. The everyday sense of the word 'depression' is ordinary English and is not covered by this source.

claims.statement: A period of raised activity is described as a distinct stretch of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood together with increased activity or energy, accompanied by features that may include reduced need for sleep, increased or pressured speech, racing ideas, distractibility, grandiosity, impulsivity, increased goal-directed activity, and involvement in activities carrying a high potential for painful consequences; the conventional duration thresholds are at least seven days for mania, or less where it led to hospital admission, and at least four days for hypomania, and psychotic features occur in mania and not in hypomania.
claims.scope: The descriptive features and duration conventions set out in a 2025 Lancet seminar on bipolar disorder. Used in this lesson to say what would be described, never to establish that any case meets a threshold.
claims.uncertainty: The duration thresholds are conventions of a classification system and have been contested, particularly the four-day minimum for hypomania. Meeting a duration threshold is not by itself a diagnosis.

claims.statement: Depressive and elevated features can run inside the same episode, and how often that is recorded depends heavily on the criteria applied: in 672 non-psychotic mood episodes from twelve Korean centres, 5.8% met the DSM-5 mixed-features specifier while 31.7% met broader research criteria, with irritable mood the commonest elevated feature at 90.8%; anxiety, agitation, and irritability in mixed states contribute to misdiagnosis and to raised suicide risk.
claims.scope: The prevalence figures describe hospitalised patients at twelve centres in the Republic of Korea between 2013 and 2016 and are cited to show how far the count moves with the definition, not as a general rate. The misdiagnosis and suicide-risk statement comes from a 2025 seminar summarising the bipolar literature.
claims.uncertainty: The definition of mixed features is actively contested, and the fivefold gap between the two criteria sets in a single sample is itself the evidence of that. A retrospective chart review can undercount features that were present but not recorded.

claims.statement: Delusions or hallucinations occur within depressive episodes, commonly with nihilistic content, and are described as mood-congruent or mood-incongruent with precedence given to incongruent features when both are present; 14.7% of people meeting criteria for major depression in the United States Epidemiologic Catchment Area study had a history of psychotic features, a European sample gave 18.5%, about a quarter of hospitalised depressed patients met criteria for the psychotic form, and in one well-characterised sample 27% of 130 diagnoses were initially incorrect because the psychosis rather than the mood disorder was missed.
claims.scope: Figures as reported in a 2013 review in Schizophrenia Bulletin, each attached in the lesson to the population it came from. The misdiagnosis figure describes one research sample of people already known to have psychotic depression and does not estimate how often records in general are wrong.
claims.uncertainty: The prevalence figures come from studies of different populations, eras, and criteria and are not directly comparable with one another. Classification of congruence has changed across editions.

claims.statement: Depressive episodes carry measurable change in attention, in memory and learning, in executive function, and in psychomotor processing speed, and residual cognitive deficits persist after the episode resolves, with a documented effect on occupational and social functioning.
claims.scope: Clinical practice guidance on cognitive impairment in major depressive disorder published in the Indian Journal of Psychiatry in 2025. The lesson uses it to justify describing concentration as an element in its own right, not to predict any individual's course.
claims.uncertainty: The size of the residual deficit varies between studies and populations, and guideline statements summarise a heterogeneous literature. Subjective complaints of poor concentration and measured performance do not always agree, and this source does not settle that relationship.

claims.statement: People who have had raised-activity episodes frequently do not recognise them as such: among 40 Dutch adults with a lifetime bipolar diagnosis confirmed by structured interview, 82.5% recognised a past depressive episode while 22.5% recognised a past hypomanic or manic one and 17.5% had ever consulted a health professional about it, and those who did not recognise the periods described them as pleasant and productive stretches, as part of their personality, or as the result of circumstances.
claims.scope: A reappraisal of 40 respondents drawn from a Netherlands general-population survey and re-interviewed in 2001 and 2002. The percentages describe that sample and not any clinic population.
claims.uncertainty: The sample is small, the reappraisal is now more than two decades old, and diagnoses were made against DSM-IV. The finding supports taking a person's own framing of a past period as weak evidence of its nature; it does not establish that any particular remembered period was an episode.

claims.statement: A retrospectively reported episode carries real signal with imprecise boundaries: in 68 participants of an Oregon cohort, concurrent symptom scores collected inside periods later reported as depressive episodes were higher than those collected between them by a medium-to-large margin, while 49.1% of those within-episode reports reached the scale's clinical cut-off, and the length of the recall interval did not significantly change the association.
claims.scope: One United States cohort followed with repeated symptom questionnaires, examining depressive episodes only. The lesson uses it to justify recording a remembered episode at the strength of a report and neither discarding it nor promoting it.
claims.uncertainty: The study concerns recall of depressive episodes and measures nothing about recall of periods of raised activity, which other evidence suggests is recalled far less well. The sample is small and drawn from a cohort recruited in adolescence.

claims.statement: Establishing a past hypomanic period from the patient's account alone is difficult, corroborative history from someone else helps confirm it, and the interval between a diagnosis of unipolar depression and a diagnosis of bipolar disorder can extend to about ten years.
claims.scope: A 2025 Lancet seminar summarising the bipolar-disorder literature. The delay figure describes cohorts of people who eventually received a bipolar diagnosis and says nothing about any individual.
claims.uncertainty: Reported diagnostic delays vary widely between studies and health systems. An informant's account has its own limits, set by what that person was in a position to observe.

terms.definition: The set of changes a person brings to a clinical contact, described element by element with what changed, over what period, and where the information came from. A presentation is a description of a person at a time; it is not a diagnosis and does not name one.

One described change within a presentation, such as the sleep, the appetite, or the ability to hold a thought. In this lesson each element is written with three things attached: what changed, its time course, and its source.

A statement of what was reported or observed, written so that another clinician who was not present could have written the same words from the same material. A description carries no conclusion about what the findings mean.

alignment.note: The description, inference, and interpretation distinction is owned by the earlier outcome on description and inference, and this lesson keeps that meaning unchanged. What this lesson adds is the practical consequence: a description that has lost its source has stopped being a description, because nobody downstream can reproduce it.

terms.definition: A conclusion you have drawn from findings, such as calling a person withdrawn, guarded, or minimising. Inferences are legitimate and useful, and they belong in your impression rather than on a line that reports what happened.

alignment.note: Adopted unchanged from the earlier outcome on description and inference. This lesson uses it only to enforce one rule: an inference may not occupy a finding line, because a later reader cannot tell it apart from something that was seen or said.

terms.definition: Where an element came from, which in this lesson is exactly one of three things: the person's own report, another person's report or record, or your own observation. Inference is not a source.

An account of a person's presentation given by someone else, such as a relative, housemate, employer, or an earlier clinical record. Its value is set by the informant's vantage point: what they were actually in a position to see, and over what period.
The four temporal facts an element needs: when it began and how sharply, how long it has run, what pattern it follows within a day or a week, and whether it is worsening, steady, or easing.

A finding that a change is absent because the question was put and answered in the negative. It is written down, and it is different from a record that simply says nothing, which leaves a later reader unable to tell absence from an unasked question.
The sustained emotional state a person reports from the inside, holding across hours to weeks. In a description it is written from the person's own account, with its own time course.

alignment.note: The mood and affect distinction is owned by the earlier mental-status observation outcome, and this lesson adopts it unchanged. Ordinary speech treats the two words as interchangeable, which is why the worked example names them side by side at the point where a reported state and an observed expression have to go on separate lines.

terms.definition: The moment-to-moment expression of emotional state that an observer sees during a bounded stretch of time, including its range and how it moves. In a description it is written as an observation, and its time course is the length of the contact.

alignment.note: Adopted unchanged from the earlier mental-status observation outcome. This lesson uses the distinction for one purpose: mood and affect are separate lines with separate sources, so a later reader can see one move while the other does not.

terms.definition: A word carrying two meanings that get exchanged without notice. In ordinary speech it names a low mood, usually about something and usually passing. In clinical use a major depressive episode names a syndrome requiring depressed mood or loss of interest and pleasure most days for at least two weeks, with several further changes and dysfunction alongside. This lesson writes low mood for the first and spells the syndrome out in full for the second.

The described state of persistently lowered mood, written as an element with its own onset, duration, pattern, and source. Using this phrase keeps a description from implying the clinical syndrome before anyone has established it.
Loss of interest in activities and loss of the pleasure they previously gave. It is described separately from low mood because the two can begin at different times and can move separately.
Waking earlier than intended and not returning to sleep. Described with a time, a frequency, and whether sleep returns, because those three are what allow a later comparison.

Mood raised or expansive beyond the person's usual state, described as part of a distinct period that also carries increased activity or energy. In a description it is dated and sourced like any other element, and naming what kind of episode it belongs to is a separate task.

Mood in which small provocations produce anger or impatience out of proportion to the person's usual response. It is the alternative direction the same element can take alongside elevated mood, and on its own it discriminates very little, since it accompanies a wide range of states.

Depressive and elevated features running inside the same episode. How often this is recorded depends strongly on which criteria are applied, so a description states the co-occurring features and their dates and leaves the labelling to a later step.

Delusions or hallucinations occurring within a mood episode. They are called mood-congruent when their content fits the mood state and mood-incongruent when it does not. Their absence counts as a finding only when the question was actually asked.

Slowing or agitation in movement, speech, and the speed of responding, described from what an observer saw during a bounded contact. It is recorded separately from what the person reports about energy, because the two have different sources and can move separately.

Specific things a person did before and now does differently, each with a date and a source, covering work, study, household tasks, self-care, and contact with other people. A single global rating of function is not a description of it.

Attribution and provenance

Lesson identity

Original contribution

The lesson prose, the fictional people R., M., K., P., A., and D., the referral sentence, the transcript fragments, the observations, the referral and discharge documents, the invented weights and dates, the follow-up appointment, all tables, prompts, feedback, assessment items, rubrics, and glossary definitions were created for EmbeddedKnowledge and are contributed under CC BY 4.0 by the accountable principal. No third-party visual, media, dataset, quotation, or adapted expression is included, and the pack carries no assets.

R. is the shared teaching case of this psychiatry block and appears in other lessons of the same module. The facts used here are the block's canonical ones; the referral letter, the twenty-minute observation record, and the eleven-week follow-up are detail added by this lesson and are consistent with them. The follow-up is presented in the text as a supposition, since its purpose is to show what a description makes measurable and not to fix a course of events.

The published learner-facing pack for PSY-WEL-001 was consulted for psychiatry conventions and boundary wording, and PREM-STA-001 for pack structure. No review or adjudication artifact from any prior lesson was consulted, and no prior lesson prose, example, assessment item, or structured artifact was copied into this pack.

Terminology continuity

The psychiatry terminology ledger was read before the glossary was designed. It holds six terms, all owned by PSY-WEL-001, and this lesson defines none of them, so no collision with a published lesson arises.

Four entries declare an alignment block naming a lesson of this block that is not yet published, because the block brief assigns ownership of those terms elsewhere and this lesson adopts rather than redefines them:

  • description and inference — adopt from PSY-WEL-002, which owns the description, inference, and interpretation distinction. This lesson keeps the meaning unchanged and adds only the rule that an inference may not occupy a finding line.
  • mood and affect — adopt from PSY-INT-004, which owns the distinction. The worked example names the two words side by side at the point where a reported state and an observed expression have to be written on separate lines.

Reviewers should note that both owning lessons are unauthored at the time of this candidate, so those alignment declarations are forward references and cannot yet be checked against a published definition.

Source use and rights

Seven sources support the factual claims. All were used for facts only, followed by independent instructional structure and original expression. Complete locators, use records, rights evidence, and dated agent-access checks appear in references.json, and each claim's scope and uncertainty appear in claims.json.

  • Carty and Escalona, Brief Review of Major Depressive Disorder for Primary Care Providers: which changes make up a major depressive episode, the two-week minimum, the requirement that they be present most days, and the spread of dysfunction.
  • Singh and colleagues, Bipolar disorder (Lancet seminar, 2025): the descriptive features of a period of raised activity, the mania and hypomania duration conventions, psychotic features in mania and not hypomania, anxiety and agitation and irritability in mixed states, diagnostic delay, and the value of corroborative history.
  • Shim and colleagues, The prevalence and diagnostic classification of mixed features in patients with major depressive episodes: 5.8% against 31.7% on the same 672 non-psychotic episodes depending on the criteria applied, irritable mood as the commonest elevated feature, and reclassification as anxious distress or a personality disorder.
  • Rothschild, Challenges in the Treatment of Major Depressive Disorder With Psychotic Features: the frequency of psychotic features in depressive episodes across named populations, nihilistic delusional content, the mood-congruence distinction, and the finding that 27% of 130 diagnoses in one sample were initially wrong because the psychosis was missed. Only the epidemiological and diagnostic content was used; the paper is a treatment review and none of its treatment material appears in this lesson.
  • Singh and colleagues, Clinical practice guidelines on the assessment and management of cognitive impairment in major depressive disorder: the affected cognitive domains, the persistence of residual deficits after an episode resolves, and the effect on occupational and social functioning. This source is displayed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, a licence this project does not adapt or redistribute, so it was used for facts only and no expression was reused.
  • Regeer and colleagues, Low self-recognition and awareness of past hypomanic and manic episodes in the general population: the recognition and consultation percentages in 40 Dutch adults with a structured-interview bipolar diagnosis, and the explanations non-recognisers gave for those periods.
